claims.text: The initial material is equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW.
NbMoTaW has high elevated-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility.
Substituting approximately 10–20 at.% Ti for one BCC constituent will produce discrete HCP precipitates in a continuous BCC NbMoTaW matrix.
The ratio of HCP-derived to BCC-derived elements can be used to control strength and ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Introducing HCP-stabilizing elements into NbMoTaW will locally lower dislocation-core energy.
Introducing HCP-stabilizing elements will increase the number of available slip systems.
Lower dislocation-core energy and altered slip activity will enhance room-temperature plasticity.
A dual-phase microstructure can combine improved room-temperature ductility with high strength.
A continuous BCC matrix will preserve the modified alloy's high-temperature strength.
A continuous BCC matrix will preserve irradiation resistance by maintaining phase stability and limiting defect coarsening.
The Ti-substituted alloy will have greater room-temperature strain to failure than untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti-substituted alloy will retain high-temperature yield strength comparable to untreated NbMoTaW up to approximately 1600 °C.
The Ti-substituted alloy will resist irradiation-induced amorphization better than untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti-substituted alloy will resist irradiation-enhanced precipitation better than untreated NbMoTaW.
The proposed improvements apply from room temperature to approximately 1600 °C wherever the BCC phase remains stable.
The proposed irradiation benefit applies under helium implantation or heavy-ion irradiation relevant to extreme environments.
The HCP precipitates may coarsen at high temperature or under irradiation if their fraction and chemistry are not optimized.
Baseline and Ti-substituted alloys should be processed with comparable thermal histories and tested mechanically and under controlled irradiation.
Failure to improve room-temperature ductility, substantial high-temperature strength loss, or greater irradiation damage would falsify the hypothesis.
